The Master of Art in User Experience/User Interface (UX/UI) Design is a stackable master's that combines the four-course Graduate Certificate in User Experience Design, developed by WRT, and the four-course Graduate Certificate in User Interface Design, created by ART, augmented by two additional courses.
The thirty-credit program will prepare students for meaningful careers in the burgeoning fields of UX/UI.
This online accelerated dual-focus curriculum offers students— including those with full-time jobs—a flexible path to gaining proficiency with the tools and approaches of the closely related fields of UX and UI research and design, opening a broad range of lucrative career opportunities.
Students emerge from this program as versatile professionals capable of addressing complex design challenges.
Their skills span from the intricate details of UI elements to the strategic considerations of holistic user experiences.
Armed with the knowledge of both UX and UI, graduates become adept at designing solutions that merge aesthetics, functionality, and human-centered values.
The program is unique in its emphasis on the ethical implications of research and design processes and products.

The UX Certificate nurtures an understanding of user behavior, needs, and expectations through rigorous research, ensuring accessibility and accessible design.
UX courses guide students in creating designs that prioritize inclusivity, social justice, sustainability, and user well-being.
They also offer students cutting-edge approaches to UX writing and interaction design.
The UI Design Certificate provides students with the crucial knowledge, and the technical and practical skills, to become proficient UI designers.
Students will create interface projects integrating branding, animation, patternmaking, and front-end visualizations to depict intuitive user experiences, enabling them to craft interactions that leave a lasting impact.
Students in the Master's Program are able to take UI Visual Principles for Non-designers, which helps them develop a unique approach to the design process with the user interface experience in mind (advanced designers may also select an approved elective from other URIO offerings).
The two certificates then culminate in WRT/ART 509: UX/UI Portfolio.

In this cross-listed course (WRT and ART), students integrate and apply the knowledge and skills they have gained in their UX and UI Design Certificate courses to create compelling, effective, polished portfolios that demonstrate their expertise to potential employers and clients.
Additionally, the course will focus on professionalization for careers in UX, UI, and related design fields.
Graduates of this program will have the capability to examine how individuals navigate real-life scenarios, empowering them to enhance experiences by creating new design-centered connections.
They will possess the abilities to recognize limitations and openings for enhancing interactions between objects, systems—whether virtual or physical—as well as the people who interact with them.
In an ever-evolving technological landscape, the Master of Arts in UX/UI Design equips students to stand at the forefront of innovation, transcending traditional boundaries between the two fields.
Graduates leave prepared to meet industry demands and set new standards that enrich the lives of users, making a positive impact on society.

Strategy 1 in the Agenda for Change is deeply embedded in the goals and learning outcomes of this program.
The Master's in UX/UI emphasizes the application of ethical, collaborative design practices to solve real-world problems, focusing on inclusive design, design justice, person-first design, and designing for the social good.
Students will learn to engage in design processes that prioritize the needs and perspectives of diverse user populations.
By understanding the principles of inclusive design, they will acquire the ability to create solutions that cater to a wide range of users, ensuring accessibility and usability for all.

1 year 30 30 1 0 No UX Certificate WRT 501: Ethical Foundations of UX explores the ethical considerations and responsibilities involved in designing digital experiences for users.
Through a combination of theoretical concepts, case studies, and practical exercises, students will gain an understanding of the ethical challenges faced by user experience designers and develop strategies to create user- centered and ethically sound designs.
Students will explore UX as a research and development method, especially as it relates to inclusive design and design justice.
Students will learn about foundational concepts in UX design, including terminology, history, and evolution of the field.
Using a critical lens, students will investigate issues of social justice, equity, sustainability, accessibility, and inclusion.
WRT 502: UX Research and Methods is an introduction to methods, research design, and data analysis in user experience projects, and aims to prepare professionals for designing, conducting, analyzing, and reporting their own user research studies.

This course will train students in how to determine the best methods and metrics for their projects, as well as design studies for effective data collection.
This course will also teach students how to communicate research results for decision-making purposes to a variety of stakeholders.
Students in this course will gain hands-on practice at every phase of the user research process, from identifying design problems or questions to developing their own test protocols, recruiting users, conducting user tests, and analyzing their results.
WRT 503: UX and Microcopy Writing is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the role and impact of effective writing in user-centered design.
Through a combination of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students will develop the skills necessary to create clear, concise, and engaging microcopy for digital interfaces and interactions.
WRT 504: Interaction Design focuses on the process of rapid, iterative design that keeps real people at the heart of creating content—a philosophy and design approach known as human-centered design.

Students in this course will learn agile design workflows, conduct rapid prototyping and wireframing, and share reflections on the process and results of user research meaningfully for public and industry audiences.
Students will gain hands-on, applied knowledge of the human-centered design process by creating their own design and refining it based on user feedback.

ART 505: UI Design: Styling and Prototyping introduces students to the theory and practice of user interface design, focusing on visual communication tools and skills to facilitate prototyping.
Students will acquire a knowledge of the UI design thinking process, centering on the user's visual experience, which is crucial to how users interact with an interface.
Students will learn how to collaborate as a visual designer in creating interactive screen-based interfaces for websites and apps, creating visual components while considering their interactive properties, look and feel, responsiveness and interactivity and recognizing the multiple human factors, audiences and contexts that govern their design decisions.
ART 506: UI Motion Design introduces motion design in user experience within a framework of the three foundational principles of communication, orientation, and correlation.
Students will learn how motion design can complement visual affordances to provide users with more meaningful experiences and interactions.
It explores motion design as a sequence of movements that affects the user’s perception of any interface a user interacts with.

ART 507: UI Icon Design introduces and develops the skills needed to conceptualize and design icons for user interfaces.
The context, design and application of UI icons will be critiqued based on the effectiveness and appropriateness of the design language.
Students will learn to generate UI icon sets through a process that explores visual rhetoric and shape form creation through a logical visual process.
This course provides an overview of the nature and purpose of icons in user interfaces, their key characteristics, and aesthetic rules commonly used in websites and apps.
ART 508: UI Information Visualization Design focuses on the design, creation, understanding, application, and evaluation of information visualization for user interfaces.
Students will learn strategies and techniques to organize, visualize and communicate information and how to implement them on multiple platforms.

Students will gain an understanding of the importance of the interface focusing on users and the graphical depictions of complex information for more efficient and effective processing, leading to faster and more accurate results.The course reflects upon the many ways in which information design is carried out to improve the student’s own design process, and to convey meaning from information, with the primary focus placed on educating the viewer through their visualization experiences.
Integrated Courses WRT/ART 509: UX/UI Portfolio enables students to develop the visual and technical skills to create a professional and attractive electronic portfolio.
The final product will combine their undergraduate and graduate graphic, interaction, or experience design work for review by potential employers or clients.
The class will teach students how to objectively review and revise existing works and the protocol or design principles needed for portfolio creation.
Instructors will work individually with students and help them choose pieces that best represent their strengths as a designer.

Students may take the following or seek approval for another URI Online course to serve as an elective: ART 510: UI Visual Principles for Non-Designers introduces students with little or no background or formal design training to the fundamentals of the field. "UI Visual Principles for Non-Designers" aids students in developing a unique approach to the design process and helps them understand the steps necessary to complete projects from the initial brief to the final piece.
Students will learn to apply design thinking and visual skills to meaningful communications and user interface experiences while understanding the importance of the audience and context in every decision-making.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report 2023-2024-02 - Proposed amendments to Appendix G Faculty Senate - March 28, 2024 Rationale: The primary change proposed relates to increasing clarity in the reference to Policy #80-1 in Appendix G.
When the Faculty Senate authorized migrating administrative policies previously listed in Appendix G to the Administrative Policies website, an error was introduced wherein Policy #80-1 regarding Faculty Senate jurisdiction over policies was inadvertently deleted.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee found no evidence that the Faculty Senate ever rescinded the missing Policy, gave an informational report on this matter to the Faculty Senate on October 19, 2023, and reposted a link to the policy in Appendix G along with a brief explanation about what had occurred.
Because Policy #80-1 codifies a power and duty of the Faculty Senate relating to the approval of administrative policies, it is appropriate and important to include not only a link to the policy in this Appendix but also clear details about the content of the policy and the codified role of the Faculty Senate in the administrative policy development and approval process.

Additional changes aim to 1) accurately reflect the relationship between academic policies and collective bargaining agreements and state and federal statutes and regulations, 2) clarify the nature of the University Manual as the official policy document where policies are not only described but also codified through legislative processes, and 3) correct an error in fact (it is not the President of the Faculty Senate, but rather the entire body of the Faculty Senate that has the authority to jointly own policies).
Proposed changes to Appendix G: University Policies In recognition that the University Manual has been created through the framework of shared governance between the university faculty and administration under the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees, it is the source of information regarding the structure, rights, regulations, and practices that govern university life.
The Manual is considered to be the official university policy document articulating shared governance and, as such, takes precedence over other internal policy statements inconsistent or conflicting with the Manual.

Academic policies, with the exception of those mandated by collective bargaining agreements or by government at state or federal levels statutes or regulations, are legislated by Faculty Senate and Presidential action, and are articulated and codified in the various Chapters and Appendices of this Manual.
Administrative policies are set forth within the framework of this Appendix and maintained by the Office of the Vice President of Administration and Finance, with oversight by the Administrative Policy Committee.
Administrative policies with provisions that fall under Faculty Senate jurisdiction also require approval by the Page 1 of 2 FSEC Report 2023-2024-02 Bill #23-24-20

Faculty Senate.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee shall determine if some or all of the provisions of an administrative policy fall under Faculty Senate jurisdiction.
Policy #80-1 (“Establishing Administrative Policy”) Research and intellectual property (IP) policies are academic and administrative policies set forth in Section 4 of this Appendix maintained by the Office of the Vice President for Research and Economic Development.
Although many research policies are academic in nature affecting the faculty as a whole, many other research policies are treated as administrative in nature, mandated by requirements of federal and state granting authorities.

In addition, the policy provides information regarding regular review, promulgation, policy repositories, and archiving.

Methods of Instruction The CAC has adopted the following definitions of methods of instruction: Definitions for Methods of Instruction Revision of definitions in the CAC's Three Hundred and Seventh Report (October 13, 1993) Lecture: A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small- group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
Laboratory: In-class applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Recitation: Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Studio: In-class, supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which facuity instruct, assist, and critique. 2

Seminar: Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20* students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.
Independent Study: One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities.
Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Practicum: Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice.
Includes clinics, internships, ex tern ships, student teaching, field experiences.
May include regular class meetings.
Workshop: Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
Online: A course that is delivered entirely online. (CAC policy includes possibility of a required organizational session, etc.) SECTIONI Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Facuity Senate A.

Executive Summary 1.
Expansion of CRCA Membership: The CRCA expanded its membership to include five new research-active, non-senator voting members and added the Vice President for Research and Economic Development as an ex-officio non-voting member.
This change aims to diversify perspectives within the committee, increase representation from various disciplines, and strengthen links to current research challenges and the university administration. 2.
Review of Indirect Cost Expenditures: The report analyzed the FY2023 overhead expenses, revealing a substantial gap between expected indirect cost recovery and the actual overhead revenue allocation.

Suggestions for improvement include optimizing the indirect cost recovery process, developing a transparent methodology for allocating indirect costs and enhancing detailed reporting and monitoring to improve transparency and strategic investment. 3.
Analysis of the Office of Research Operations: The operational review highlighted underfunding and staffing issues in the Office of Research Development (ORD), retention challenges, and the need for improved support for faculty in research activities.
Recommendations include hiring new positions as suggested by both a faculty survey and an external review and reevaluating the centralization of research support. 4.
Issues in Sponsored Research Operations: Challenges in managing larger, multi- institutional projects and bottlenecks in IRB reviews were identified as reducing productivity.
Recommendations focus on improving staffing levels and response times in the Office of Sponsored Research (OSP) to enhance research productivity. 5.
Impact of ITS Operations on Research: The current IT policies were evaluated for their impact on research productivity.
Recommendations include creating

streamlined services for software installation requests and providing guidelines for data backup prior to the installation of monitoring software. 6.
Conclusions and Recommendations: The report concludes by summarizing the significant findings and reiterating critical recommendations.

II.
Introduction The Annual Report of the CRCA for the year 2024 documents the pivotal advancements and sustained efforts in reinforcing the research and creative endeavors at the University of Rhode Island (URI).
This report, prepared by a dedicated team led by Sen.
Bahram Nassersharif, Acting Chair, underlines the critical activities and strategic initiatives undertaken by the CRCA to cultivate a robust research culture at the university.
The CRCA's responsibilities, deeply embedded in URI's academic fabric as delineated in Appendix C of the URI University Manual, encompass a broad spectrum of functions.

These include advocating for and supporting the diverse spectrum of research and creative activities that define the scholarly community at URI.
The committee acts as an essential bridge between the university administration and its vibrant intellectual community, advising on policies, supporting infrastructure needs, and fostering an environment conducive to cutting- edge research and innovation.
This year's report highlights several key developments including the strategic expansion of the committee’s membership, aimed at enhancing the diversity of perspectives and bolstering the representation from various academic disciplines.
Such changes are designed not only to enrich the committee's deliberations but also to align closely with the university's strategic goals of fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and responsiveness to emerging research challenges.
Through a detailed account of the CRCA's operations, this introduction sets the stage for a comprehensive understanding of the committee’s objectives, challenges, and the substantial impact of its work on the university’s broader strategic ambitions.

This narrative provides a contextual backdrop for the discussions and recommendations that follow in the subsequent sections of this report.
The mandates of the CRCA, as outlined in Appendix C of the URI University Manual, highlight its comprehensive responsibilities and functions:

CRCA Charges ● Advocacy and Support for Research and Creative Activities: The CRCA is tasked with promoting a comprehensive understanding of research, creative, and scholarly work.
This includes enhancing the overall well-being of such activities at URI by identifying and addressing challenges that hinder these efforts.
The committee provides recommendations for improving the management of research affairs and acts as an advisory body to the Vice President for Research and Economic Development. ● Library and Open Access: Acting as a liaison between the University Library and the faculty, the CRCA advises on matters of general faculty concern regarding the library.
It plays a consultative role in assessing the library's long-range needs and the adequacy of its budget and advises on the implementation and interpretation of URI’s Open-Access Policy.
This includes resolving disputes concerning the policy and recommending changes to the Faculty Senate. ● Competitive Grants Subcommittee: This subcommittee of the CRCA solicits proposals from faculty and awards financial support on a competitive basis for faculty development and proposal development programs.

These programs support various faculty needs, including salaries, fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment. ● Center Review Subcommittee: Responsible for reviewing applications for new centers and institutes as well as the continuing authorization of existing ones.
This subcommittee ensures that such entities meet their goals and contribute effectively to the university’s research environment.
III.
Expansion of CRCA Membership CRCA plays a crucial role in shaping the institution's research policies, fostering an environment that supports scholarly endeavors, and ensuring the distribution of research-related resources effectively aligns with the university's strategic goals.
The recent changes made in the Senate, specifically expanding the committee's membership to include five new research-active but non-senator voting members, as well as adding the Vice President for Research and Economic Development as an ex officio non-voting member, have significant implications for the governance of research at URI.

Rationale for Expanded Membership ● Enhanced Diversity of Perspectives: By incorporating five new research- active but non-senator members, the committee benefits from a broader range of insights and experiences.
These members, being active researchers, bring a fresh, on-the-ground perspective that can contribute to more informed and effective decision-making regarding research policies and resource allocation.

● Increased Representation from Various Disciplines: Research-active members likely come from diverse academic backgrounds and disciplines.
This variety ensures that the unique needs and challenges of different research areas are understood and considered, leading to more comprehensive and inclusive research policies. ● Direct Link to Current Research Challenges: Active researchers are more likely to be aware of the latest trends, challenges, and opportunities in research, including funding, technology, and interdisciplinary collaboration.
Their contributions can help the committee stay relevant and responsive to the evolving research landscape. ● Strengthening Research Culture: Including members who are directly engaged in research activities can enhance the committee’s role in advocating for a robust research culture.
This can lead to more effective strategies to foster research and creative activities across the university. ● Connection with University Administration: The addition of the Vice President for Research and Economic Development as an ex officio member provides a direct link to the university’s senior administration.

This connection can facilitate smoother implementation of committee decisions and better alignment of research initiatives with the university’s strategic objectives.
Expected Impacts from This Change ● Improved Policy Development: With inputs from diverse and active researchers, the committee is likely to develop policies that are more attuned to the actual needs of the research community.
This can lead to more effective use of resources and better support for cutting-edge research activities. ● Enhanced Communication and Collaboration: The presence of a wider range of members, especially the inclusion of a high-ranking administrative officer like the Vice President, can improve communication between researchers and the university administration.

This could lead to more collaborative efforts across departments and disciplines. ● Greater Advocacy for Research Needs: The expanded membership can strengthen the committee’s ability to advocate for the needs of the research community, potentially leading to enhanced support from the university in terms of funding, infrastructure, and administrative assistance. ● More Informed Decision Making: The direct involvement of active researchers ensures that the committee's decisions are informed by up-to- date knowledge of the research environment, technology advancements, and the global research agenda. ● Broader Impact on University Strategy: With strategic inputs from diverse academic fields and a direct link to university administration, the committee’s influence on the overall university strategy could increase,

aligning more closely with national and international research priorities and funding landscapes.
Going forward, these changes are expected to dynamically enhance the functionality and impact of the Committee on Research and Creative Activities at URI, fostering a more vibrant, responsive, and interdisciplinary research environment that aligns with both the academic and practical needs of the university.
This, in turn, should bolster URI's reputation as a leading research institution.

Review of Indirect Cost Expenditures Based on the information provided in the FY2023 Overhead Report, here is an analysis of the indirect cost report and suggestions for improvements: 1.
Indirect cost recovery comparison: ○ URI reported $108,622,286 in research expenditures during 2022- 2023. ○ At an indirect cost rate of 57.5%, the expected indirect cost recovery should be approximately $62,457,814 ($108,622,286 x 0.575). ○ The actual overhead revenue allocation reported in the document is $16,028,277. ○ There is a significant gap between the expected indirect cost recovery and the actual overhead revenue allocation, indicating that URI may not be fully recovering its indirect costs. 2.

Allocation of indirect costs: ○ The report did not provide a breakdown of the indirect cost distribution. ○ It is unclear from the report how these allocations are determined and whether they align with the actual overhead distribution formulas. 3.
Transparency and detail: ○ The report provides a high-level summary of indirect cost allocations and expenditures but lacks detailed breakdowns for some units. ○ Increasing transparency by providing more granular information on how indirect costs are spent particularly by the Division of Research and the Division of Finance and Administration. 4.
Strategic investment of indirect cost recovery: ○ The report indicates that a significant portion of indirect cost recovery is used for payroll and fringe benefits.
However, no additional information is provided as to who is being paid from overhead funds. ○ URI should consider strategically investing a portion of the indirect cost recovery in initiatives that support and enhance research activities, such as infrastructure improvements, seed funding for new projects, or direct support of faculty who generate overhead. 5.
Monitoring and analysis:

○ URI should regularly monitor and analyze its overhead expenditures to identify trends, variances, and opportunities for improvement. ○ Comparing actual indirect cost recovery against budgeted amounts and benchmarking against peer institutions can provide valuable insights.
Suggestions for improvement: 1.
Review and optimize the indirect cost recovery process to ensure that URI is capturing all eligible indirect costs associated with research activities. 2.
Under the New Budget Model, develop a transparent methodology for allocating indirect costs to administrative units based on their contribution to research support and directly to faculty who generate that indirect cost. 3.
Provide more detailed reporting on indirect cost utilization within each unit to enhance transparency and accountability. 4.
Implement regular monitoring and analysis of indirect cost recovery to identify trends, variances, and opportunities for improvement.
By addressing these areas, URI can improve its indirect cost recovery, ensure transparent allocation of funds, and strategically invest in research support and enhancement initiatives.

Analysis of the Office of Research Operations ● A.

Operational Review ○ The committee discussed the research division’s administrative and operational efficiency. ○ Office of Research Development ■ ORD is currently under-funded and under-resourced.
There are retention issues, with very high turnover, as well as a need to hire new positions.
The committee acknowledges that the President and interim VPR are aware of the situation. ■ A survey of faculty perceptions of research support was conducted under former VPR Peter Snyder.
The Committee does not have access to the original survey but met with Melissa McCarthy to discuss the questions and outcomes.
The main finding was the need for more research support staff. ■ An external review was conducted in 2021 by the National Organization of Research Development’s (NORDP) Program for External Evaluation of Research Development (PEERD).
The committee received a copy of this report in mid-April.
The report recommends greater investment in research support and increased staffing, stating, “We strongly suggest URI consider

structural and staffing changes to [ORD] to strengthen its centralized role in the research enterprise.” ■ Individualized help with research development (e.g. grant proposals) is often not available to faculty when they need it. ■ Significant concerns exist about the new practice of hiring full- time remote staff who are not located near URI, such as the new AVP for Research. ○ Institutional Review Board ■ There are currently long delays with IRB review, with decision making sporadic and difficult to understand.
In some cases this has led to missed deadlines, and projects needing to be changed or moved outside of URI. ■ There are concerns that IRB reviewers do not have the necessary background to make decisions. ■ The committee wanted to investigate this further by inviting the IRB staff or VPR to join a committee meeting.
Recommend that the CRCA continue to investigate this issue. ○ Pre-award to Post-award process ■ This process is severely challenging for faculty.
Funds are difficult to locate.
There are many issues with different number codes being used to track awards and not cross-linked.

Pre- award is managed by the Research office; Post-award is managed by the Controller. ○ Centralization and Decentralization of research support ■ Many colleges have their own support staff for writing grant proposals.
The committee took steps towards gathering information about research staff in individual colleges and discussed whether research support should remain centralized under IBB. ● B.
